question: You declare a tool with a JSON `input_schema` and Claude calls it. What does the Anthropic API guarantee about the `tool_use.input` payload?
options: It conforms to the schema (valid JSON syntax, declared keys, types, required fields, enum values).
It is semantically correct — line items sum to totals and fields are placed in the right keys.
It will be returned only when Claude is fully confident, otherwise the API returns plain text.
It is automatically validated against a Pydantic model registered alongside the tool.
explanations: Correct. The API enforces JSON-syntactic and schema-shape compliance before responding.
No — the schema validates shape, not semantics. Sums and field-placement are not enforced.
No — `tool_choice` controls whether a tool is called, not the API's confidence in the payload.
No — Pydantic is a downstream validator you wire up yourself; the API doesn't know about it.

question: A team is moving from 'ask Claude for JSON in a code fence and parse it' to tool_use with a JSON schema. What problem does the migration eliminate?
options: Semantic errors in the extracted data, including line items that don't sum to totals.
Free-form text JSON parse failures (trailing commas, prose preambles, markdown leakage).
The need to specify required fields anywhere in the system.
All hallucinations, including fabricated values for missing source data.
explanations: No — semantic errors persist. Schemas validate shape, not meaning.
Correct. Tool use removes the free-form text channel for the structured payload.
No — required vs optional fields are still part of schema design.
No — fabrication of missing values is a separate problem solved by nullable fields.

question: Three different document types may arrive (invoice, purchase order, receipt). You have one extraction tool per type and want guaranteed structured output without hard-coding which schema to use. Which `tool_choice` is correct?
options: `"auto"` — let the model decide whether structured output is needed.
`"any"` — Claude must call a tool but is free to pick which one matches the document.
`{"type":"tool","name":"extract_invoice"}` — force the most common type.
Disable `tool_choice` — register all three tools and let normal generation pick.
explanations: No — `"auto"` allows Claude to reply with text instead of calling a tool, breaking the guarantee.
Correct. `"any"` guarantees a tool call while letting Claude select the matching schema.
No — forcing one schema means PO and receipt documents get extracted into the wrong shape.
No — that's `"auto"` semantics; the guarantee is lost.

question: You need `extract_metadata` to run before any enrichment step. Which `tool_choice` value enforces this?
options: `{"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"}` — force that specific tool by name.
`"any"` — Claude will pick the right one.
`"auto"` — the model already knows extraction comes first.
Set `metadata: required` on the system prompt.
explanations: Correct. Forced tool selection requires Claude to call exactly that tool on this turn.
No — with `"any"` Claude could pick a different registered tool.
No — `"auto"` lets Claude reply with text instead.
No — there is no such system prompt directive; behaviour is controlled by `tool_choice`.

question: An extraction tool's schema marks `phone_number` as required, but the source document has no phone number. What does Claude tend to do?
options: Skip the tool call entirely and reply with an error message.
Return a `tool_use` block with `phone_number` omitted; the API rejects it.
Fabricate a plausible-looking phone number to satisfy the required field.
Throw a validation exception inside the API.
explanations: No — Claude completes the tool call when forced or instructed; it doesn't error out gracefully.
Tool calls usually succeed; required fields incentivise the model to fill them rather than omit.
Correct. Required fields with no source value incentivise the model to invent a value.
No — the API doesn't validate semantically; it just enforces shape, and a fabricated string is shape-valid.

question: How do you let Claude honestly signal 'this value isn't in the source document'?
options: Add a `"confidence"` field and ask Claude to set it to 0 when unsure.
Tighten the schema with regex patterns so invalid values fail validation.
Mark the field optional (omit from `required`) or nullable (`type: ["string","null"]`).
Use `tool_choice: "auto"` so Claude can refuse to call the tool.
explanations: Confidence fields are a separate technique and don't change the fabrication incentive on required fields.
Regex patterns produce validation failures, not honest `null` values.
Correct. Optional/nullable fields let Claude return `null`, preserving the truth that data is missing.
No — refusing to call the tool breaks the structured-output contract.

question: An enum is `"category": {"enum": ["invoice","purchase_order","receipt"]}` but a credit memo arrives. What does the strict three-value enum do, and what's the recommended fix?
options: Forces a least-wrong pick (silently miscategorising); fix by adding `"unclear"` and/or `"other"` + a detail string.
Returns null for the category; fix by making the field required.
Fails the API call; fix by removing the enum constraint.
Triggers a model refusal; fix by switching to `tool_choice: "any"`.
explanations: Correct. Closed enums force a least-wrong selection; `"unclear"`/`"other"`+detail keep categories extensible.
Enums don't return null automatically; required-ness doesn't help here.
The API call succeeds — the model picks one of the allowed values, just the wrong one.
Models don't refuse on enum mismatch; they pick the closest enum value.

question: Where do format normalisation rules (date format `YYYY-MM-DD`, two-decimal currency, ISO-3166 country codes) belong?
options: Hard-coded as regex `pattern` constraints in the JSON schema.
In a downstream Pydantic model only; the prompt and schema should stay neutral.
In the prompt alongside the schema — the schema enforces shape; the prompt enforces format.
In the model name (e.g., switch to a model fine-tuned for finance documents).
explanations: Most rules aren't cleanly expressible as regex; even when expressible, schema validation failures are a worse signal than a normalised value.
Pydantic catches violations after the fact; better to have Claude produce normalised values upfront, guided by the prompt.
Correct. Format rules belong in the prompt; schema enforces shape only.
Out of scope — fine-tuning isn't part of the API surface tested here.

question: A schema requires `total`, `subtotal`, `tax`, and `line_items[].price`. The extracted row has `subtotal:80, tax:8, total:100, line_items:[{price:40},{price:40}]`. What does the schema validator say?
options: Validation fails because line items don't sum to subtotal.
Validation fails because subtotal+tax doesn't equal total.
Validation passes — schemas enforce shape, not arithmetic.
Validation passes only if `tool_choice` is set to forced.
explanations: No — schemas don't compute sums or check cross-field consistency.
No — schemas don't compute arithmetic relationships.
Correct. Every field is the right type and present; the schema is satisfied. The arithmetic error is a semantic problem.
`tool_choice` doesn't change schema validation behaviour.

question: Why might you use `"other"` plus a separate `category_detail` string field instead of a closed enum?
options: To force Claude to always pick a specific category and refuse `"other"`.
To replace the enum entirely with free-form strings.
Because enums must always include at least four values.
To keep categories extensible — Claude can return `"other"` with a detail; frequent details get promoted into the enum.
explanations: The opposite — `"other"` is for the cases where the closed list is insufficient.
No — the enum still covers known categories; `"other"` is the escape hatch.
There's no minimum-size rule for enums.
Correct. The pattern keeps the enum extensible without rewriting it on every new category.

question: An extractor's schema requires `customer_email` as a string. The source document doesn't include an email anywhere, but the harness logs show Claude returned `"john.smith@example.com"`. What's the most likely cause?
options: The Anthropic API auto-fills required fields with synthetic data when the source lacks them.
Required fields incentivise fabrication; with no source value, Claude invented a plausible email.
The extraction tool was registered with a default value of `john.smith@example.com`.
JSON schema validators inject placeholder values for missing strings.
explanations: False — the API doesn't synthesise field values.
Correct. Required fields with absent source values produce fabricated outputs; the fix is making the field nullable.
Tools don't carry default values that the API auto-fills.
JSON schema validators reject invalid input; they don't inject placeholders.

question: You register `extract_invoice`, `extract_po`, `extract_receipt`. The doc type is unknown and you must guarantee a structured payload. Which `tool_choice` is correct?
options: `{"type":"tool","name":"extract_invoice"}` — invoices are most common.
`"auto"` — Claude decides the right tool.
Set `tool_choice` to `"required"` (the API's default for guaranteed calls).
`"any"` — Claude must call a tool, free to pick the matching schema.
explanations: Forcing one schema misroutes POs and receipts.
`"auto"` lets Claude reply with text — no guarantee of a tool call.
There is no `"required"` value — the three options are `"auto"`, `"any"`, and forced by name.
Correct. `"any"` guarantees a tool call without forcing a specific schema.

question: After moving to tool_use with a strict JSON schema, the team finds that the malformed-JSON error rate dropped to zero, but the warehouse occasionally logs invoices where the line items don't sum to the total. Best next step?
options: Add a regex pattern to the `total` field to enforce two decimal places.
Switch `tool_choice` from forced to `"any"` so Claude can pick a stricter tool.
Add a downstream semantic validator (e.g., Pydantic) that re-checks `sum(line_items) == total` and routes mismatches to a review queue.
Mark `total` as nullable so Claude can return null when unsure.
explanations: Regex on a single field doesn't catch cross-field arithmetic mismatches.
Switching tool_choice doesn't change semantic correctness.
Correct. Schemas validate shape; cross-field arithmetic belongs in a downstream validator.
Nullable on `total` invites the model to return null when it's actually present — wrong remediation.

question: Which statement most accurately captures what `tool_use` with a JSON schema guarantees vs what it doesn't?
options: Guarantees both syntactic and semantic correctness — the schema is the contract.
Guarantees the model never fabricates values; semantic errors are eliminated.
Guarantees schema-shape compliance (valid JSON, declared keys, types, enums); does NOT guarantee arithmetic relationships, field-placement, or format normalisation.
Guarantees nothing without a downstream Pydantic validator running first.
explanations: Wrong — semantics are not enforced.
Wrong — fabrication of required fields is exactly the failure mode that nullable fields address.
Correct. Shape only; semantics are separate.
The shape guarantee is real and immediate; downstream validation adds semantic checks on top.

question: Source documents inconsistently format dates as `"April 4, 2026"`, `"4/4/26"`, `"04-Apr-2026"`. The schema declares `invoice_date` as a string. What's the cleanest way to ensure the warehouse receives `"2026-04-04"`?
options: Add a strict ISO-8601 regex pattern to the schema and let validation failures bubble up.
Add an instruction in the prompt: `Dates must be formatted as YYYY-MM-DD`.
Pre-process every document with a date parser before sending to Claude.
Mark `invoice_date` as nullable so Claude can return null when the format is ambiguous.
explanations: Regex catches the wrong format after the fact; the prompt rule produces the right format upfront.
Correct. Format normalisation belongs in the prompt; the schema enforces shape only.
Pre-processing duplicates work that Claude can do natively when given the rule.
Nullable doesn't address format inconsistency; it addresses missing data.

question: A classifier uses `"category": {"enum": ["invoice", "purchase_order", "receipt"]}` and you notice ~10% of warehouse rows are subtly miscategorised on edge-case documents. What's the recommended schema change?
options: Add `"unclear"` to the enum, route those rows to a human review queue, and optionally add `"other"` + a `category_detail` string for new categories.
Remove the enum constraint entirely so Claude can return any string.
Force `tool_choice: "any"` so Claude can pick a stricter classifier.
Mark `category` as nullable so Claude can leave it blank when uncertain.
explanations: Correct. `"unclear"` surfaces ambiguity; `"other"`+detail handles new categories without rewrites.
Removing the constraint loses the structured-output contract entirely.
`tool_choice` doesn't address enum design.
Nullable is for absent values, not for ambiguous classification.

question: Why might `"phone": {"type": ["string", "null"]}` be preferred over `"phone": {"type": "string"}` in an extraction schema?
options: Nullable fields are validated faster by the API.
Nullable fields force Claude to always return `null`, simplifying downstream logic.
Nullable is a syntactic requirement of `tool_use`.
Nullable fields prevent the model from fabricating values when the source document doesn't contain a phone number — Claude can return `null` honestly.
explanations: Performance isn't the reason; correctness is.
Wrong — Claude returns the value when present and `null` when absent.
It isn't required syntax; it's a design choice for honest absent-value handling.
Correct. Nullable fields preserve the truth that data is missing rather than incentivising fabrication.

question: Which combination is most appropriate when extracting a known-shape entity from a single document type, in a pipeline where the next step depends on receiving exactly that shape?
options: Define one extraction tool; set `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"extract_X"}`.
Define one extraction tool; set `tool_choice: "auto"`.
Define one extraction tool; omit `tool_choice` (use API default).
Define multiple variants of the tool and let `tool_choice: "any"` choose.
explanations: Correct. Forced tool selection guarantees the right schema runs.
`"auto"` lets Claude reply with text — no guarantee.
API default is `"auto"` — same problem.
Multiple variants of the same tool muddies the design and gives Claude unnecessary choice.

question: A schema declares `total: number` and `currency: enum[USD,EUR,GBP]`. A document is in JPY. What happens?
options: The API rejects the request because JPY isn't in the enum.
The model picks one of the allowed enum values (least-wrong selection), silently corrupting the row.
The model returns the literal string `"JPY"` and the API auto-corrects.
The harness automatically retries with a wider enum.
explanations: API doesn't reject — the model just picks an allowed value.
Correct. Closed enums force least-wrong picks; the fix is `"other"` + a `currency_detail` string.
API enforces the enum; non-allowed values aren't returned.
There's no auto-retry mechanism; the harness gets whatever the model picked.

question: In a multi-turn pipeline, you force `extract_metadata` on turn 1, then on turn 2 you want Claude to optionally call enrichment tools or summarise. What's the right `tool_choice` on turn 2?
options: Keep `{"type":"tool","name":"extract_metadata"}` — consistency matters.
`"any"` — force a tool call but let Claude pick.
`"auto"` — Claude decides whether to call a tool or reply with text.
Disable tool registration entirely on turn 2.
explanations: Forcing the same tool on turn 2 re-runs metadata extraction unnecessarily.
`"any"` forces a tool call when the right answer might be a plain text summary.
Correct. `"auto"` lets Claude pick text or a tool — appropriate when both are valid outcomes.
Disabling tools removes Claude's ability to enrich; not what you want.

question: You audit an extraction pipeline and find that for invoices missing a 'PO number' line, Claude consistently returns `"PO-00000"`. What's the schema-design root cause and fix?
options: The schema marks `po_number` as required string. Make it nullable so Claude can return `null` honestly when absent.
The model's temperature is too high. Lower it to 0.
The prompt is too long. Shorten it to under 500 tokens.
The tool is registered twice. Deregister the duplicate.
explanations: Correct. Required fields with no source value drive fabrication; nullable preserves truth.
Temperature affects randomness, not the structural fabrication incentive.
Prompt length isn't the issue.
Duplicate registration would surface as different errors, not consistent fabrication.

question: An engineer argues 'my schema has `pattern: "^[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$"` on every date field, so I don't need format rules in the prompt.' What's the most accurate critique?
options: Regex patterns are equivalent to prompt rules; either approach works.
Regex patterns reject the wrong format after the fact; a prompt rule produces the right format upfront. Most format constraints (currency precision, locale) aren't cleanly expressible as regex.
Patterns aren't supported by the Anthropic JSON-schema validator.
Patterns must live in the prompt to be enforced.
explanations: Not equivalent — the prompt rule shapes generation; regex only catches violations.
Correct. Format rules belong in the prompt; schema enforces shape only.
Patterns are supported, but that's not the relevant point.
Patterns live in the schema by definition; the issue is which is the right tool.

question: A pipeline uses `tool_choice: "auto"` with a single `extract_invoice` tool. The team reports that ~5% of invocations get a plain text response and the next stage fails. Cleanest fix?
options: Add more documentation in the system prompt instructing Claude to always call the tool.
Change `tool_choice` to `{"type":"tool","name":"extract_invoice"}` to force the tool call.
Set the model temperature to 0 to make tool-calling deterministic.
Switch to `"any"` — same effect as forced for a single tool.
explanations: Prompt instructions are advisory; `tool_choice` is a hard constraint.
Correct. Forced tool selection guarantees the call; `"auto"` is unsafe for this scenario.
Temperature affects randomness, not the structural decision to call vs reply.
`"any"` works but is less explicit than forcing by name when there's only one schema.

question: You design an `extract_contact` tool with `email`, `phone`, `address` all marked `"type": ["string", "null"]`. A source document lists only an email. What's the expected output?
options: `{"email":"x@y.com"}` (other keys omitted entirely).
An API error — required fields cannot be null.
`{"email":"x@y.com", "phone":null, "address":null}` — honest, schema-valid.
Claude refuses to call the tool because phone and address are missing.
explanations: When properties are declared, the model typically returns each key — `null` for absent values.
Nullable is the opposite of required; there's no error.
Correct. Nullable fields let Claude return `null` for absent source values.
Models don't refuse based on absent source data; they fill what they can.

question: Which scenario is best served by `tool_choice: "any"` rather than forced tool selection?
options: A single extraction tool, single document type, deterministic next step.
A coordinator that may or may not need to call a tool depending on user intent.
Multiple registered extraction tools, each tied to a different document type, where the next stage requires structured output regardless of which type arrived.
Any extraction pipeline — `"any"` is the most permissive correct choice.
explanations: Single tool + single type = forced is more explicit.
Optional tool calls are the `"auto"` use case; `"any"` forces a call.
Correct. `"any"` guarantees a structured payload while letting Claude pick the matching schema.
`"any"` isn't always correct — it forces a tool call, which `"auto"` doesn't.

question: An extractor's schema validation passes 100% of rows, but the data team flags 2% of warehouse rows as 'numerically inconsistent.' The most likely root cause is:
options: The schema is wrong and needs stricter type definitions.
The model's temperature is too high.
`tool_choice` is set to `"auto"` instead of forced.
JSON schema doesn't enforce cross-field arithmetic; semantic errors slip through and need a downstream validator.
explanations: Stricter types don't catch arithmetic.
Temperature isn't the structural cause.
Forced vs auto affects whether tool is called, not arithmetic correctness.
Correct. Schema validates shape only; arithmetic and cross-field consistency are validator territory.

question: A team wants to log every document that Claude couldn't confidently classify, separately from documents that genuinely fall outside the known categories. Best schema design?
options: Single `"other"` enum value plus a detail string — same outcome.
Add `"unclear"` to the enum for low-confidence cases AND `"other"` + `category_detail` for legitimate new categories — they serve different review queues.
Only `"unclear"` — force everything else into the closed enum.
Remove the enum — log raw classifications for human review.
explanations: Conflates two different signals (low confidence vs. new category).
Correct. The two values have distinct semantics and route to different queues.
Forces miscategorisation on legitimately new types.
Loses structured-output benefits entirely.

question: When designing an extraction tool, which fields should be marked `required` vs nullable?
options: Mark every field required — it's the safest default and forces precision.
Mark every field nullable — it's the most flexible.
Required for fields the document always contains; nullable for fields that may legitimately be absent in the source.
Required vs nullable doesn't matter; the model treats them the same.
explanations: Required fields with absent values incentivise fabrication.
Universal nullability loses the contract that key fields are present.
Correct. Match required-ness to the documents' actual structure to avoid fabrication.
The model treats them very differently; required-ness drives fill-vs-omit behaviour.

question: An invoice extractor returns shape-valid JSON but the team notices 1% of rows have the shipping address in the `billing_address` field. Best remediation?
options: Add a regex pattern to `billing_address` that rejects shipping-style strings.
Switch `tool_choice` from `"any"` to forced.

Tighten the prompt to disambiguate label-to-field mapping (e.g., 'Billing address comes from the section labelled "Bill To"; shipping from "Ship To".') and add a downstream validator that flags identical billing/shipping pairs for review.
Mark both addresses as nullable so Claude can return null for ambiguous cases.
explanations: Regex can't tell 'shipping' from 'billing' formatting — both look the same.
tool_choice doesn't address field-placement.
Correct. Field-placement errors live in the prompt and validator layers, not the schema.
Nullable doesn't address the case where Claude has data but assigned it wrong.

question: A tool's `input_schema` declares `total: number`. Claude returns `{"total": "$1,234.56"}`. What happens?
options: The harness sees a string and must JSON-parse it.
The API rejects the response and Claude retries internally.

The API enforces the schema, so the model wouldn't return this — `total` would be a number. To ensure it's `1234.56` and not `1234`, include format rules in the prompt (no symbols, two decimals) since the schema only enforces type.
The API auto-coerces the string to a number and returns 1234.56.
explanations: The payload arrives parsed in `tool_use.input`; no manual parse needed.
There's no internal retry mechanism for type mismatches at this layer.
Correct. Schema enforces type; format precision is a prompt-level concern.
API doesn't auto-coerce types; the schema enforces them as declared.

question: A team uses `tool_choice: "any"` with one registered extraction tool 'to be safe.' A reviewer suggests forcing the tool by name instead. Which most accurately captures the trade-off?
options: `"any"` is broken with single-tool setups; the API rejects it.

Forced tool selection is more explicit — future readers can tell only one schema is intended, future-proof against later tool additions (a new tool wouldn't accidentally be picked), and clearer to readers reviewing the code; `"any"` is a strictly weaker statement.
There's no difference; the two are aliases.
`"any"` is faster; forced selection adds a second round-trip.
explanations: `"any"` works fine with one tool.
Correct. Explicitness, future-proofing, and readability favour forced selection.
They differ: `"any"` lets Claude pick from all registered tools.
No round-trip difference.

question: An extractor pipeline forces `extract_invoice`. The harness finds that on rare PDFs, the resulting `tool_use.input` has `total: 100` but `line_items: [{"price": 30}, {"price": 30}]` (sums to 60). The schema validates fine. Which combination of fixes is correct?
options: Make `total` nullable; tighten enums; switch to `tool_choice: "any"`.
Lower temperature to 0; add a regex pattern on `total`; remove `line_items` from the schema.

Add a downstream validator (e.g., Pydantic) that re-checks `sum(line_items.price) == total` within tolerance, route mismatches to a review queue, and reinforce in the prompt that line items must sum to the declared total.
Switch from tool_use to free-form JSON output and parse defensively.
explanations: None of these address cross-field arithmetic.
Removing `line_items` loses the data; regex on `total` doesn't validate sums.
Correct. Cross-field consistency belongs in a downstream validator with prompt reinforcement.
That regresses to the malformed-JSON failure mode you escaped from.

question: Consider these two designs for a `currency` field. Design A: `enum: ["USD","EUR","GBP"]`. Design B: `enum: ["USD","EUR","GBP","other"]` plus nullable `currency_detail` string. Why is B preferred for a global pipeline?
options: B reduces token usage in the response.
B is required by the JSON-schema specification.
A is invalid — JSON-schema enums must include `"other"`.
B keeps the closed-enum contract for known cases AND surfaces unknown currencies (`"other"` + detail) for review, instead of forcing JPY/CHF/etc. into a least-wrong USD/EUR/GBP pick.
explanations: Token usage isn't the rationale.
Not required.
Enums don't require `"other"`; A is valid but loses the long-tail case.
Correct. The combination preserves the closed-enum contract while remaining extensible.

question: An extractor returns shape-valid JSON, but engineers notice the `notes` field is empty for documents where the source clearly has a notes paragraph. The schema marks `notes` as nullable. What's likely happening, and what's the right next step?
options: Nullable fields are silently dropped by the API; mark `notes` as required.
The model is using nullability as permission to skip work it's unsure about; reinforce in the prompt that `notes` should be populated when present in the source, only return `null` when truly absent.
The model temperature is wrong; raise it to 1.0.
Switch `tool_choice` to forced; nullable fields aren't compatible with `"any"`.
explanations: Nullable fields aren't dropped; they're passed through.
Correct. Nullability can over-encourage `null`; the prompt should clarify when to populate vs return null.
Temperature isn't the cause.
Compatibility isn't the issue; behaviour clarity is.

question: A junior engineer says: 'I don't need a Pydantic validator — the JSON schema on the tool already validates everything.' Which response is most accurate?
options: Agreed; tool_use schemas are sufficient for production.
Pydantic is only useful for type coercion, which the API already does.
JSON schema on the tool eliminates syntax errors and shape errors but does NOT enforce arithmetic, cross-field consistency, plausibility checks, or business rules — those need a downstream validator.
Pydantic is incompatible with the Anthropic API; you'd need a different SDK.
explanations: Wrong — semantic errors persist.
Pydantic does much more than coercion in this context.
Correct. Pydantic (or any semantic validator) catches what shape-only schemas can't.
No incompatibility; Pydantic operates on the parsed tool input.

question: A document arrives that's clearly an invoice, but the `"category"` field in the extracted output is `"unclear"`. Closer inspection shows the source has unusual formatting. What's the design implication?
options: The enum is wrong; remove `"unclear"` to force a confident pick.
The model temperature is too low.

`"unclear"` is doing exactly what it should — surfacing low-confidence cases to a review queue. The fix is on the review side: triage and either re-extract with a tightened prompt or flag the source for upstream cleanup.
Replace `"unclear"` with `null` to make the field optional.
explanations: Removing `"unclear"` reverts to forcing least-wrong picks.
Temperature isn't the issue.
Correct. `"unclear"` is the safety valve; the review queue is where ambiguity gets resolved.
`null` and `"unclear"` have different semantics; null = absent, unclear = ambiguous.

question: A pipeline forces `extract_invoice` and downstream Pydantic validation passes. Six months later, the team adds a new tool `extract_credit_memo` and switches `tool_choice` to `"any"` so Claude can pick. Audit shows that ~3% of incoming credit memos are now extracted as invoices with wrong fields. Most likely root cause and fix?
options: The `extract_invoice` tool description doesn't sufficiently distinguish invoice vs credit memo; Claude defaults to the more familiar tool. Tighten tool descriptions and prompt-level disambiguation rules; consider a separate classifier turn that picks the tool name, then forces it on turn 2.
Pydantic validation broke; rewrite the validators.
`"any"` is broken for two-tool setups; revert to forced.
The model temperature is causing flicker between tools; lower to 0.
explanations: Correct. Tool selection under `"any"` is driven by descriptions and prompt; ambiguity surfaces as wrong-tool selection. A two-turn pattern (classify, then force) is robust.
Pydantic isn't the issue when the wrong tool runs.
`"any"` works fine; it's a description-clarity problem.
Temperature isn't the structural cause.

question: Engineer A claims: 'JSON schema on tool_use prevents hallucinated values.' Engineer B claims: 'No, only nullable fields prevent fabrication.' Which is more accurate, and why?
options: A — schema enforcement guarantees correctness.
Neither — the API auto-detects fabrication.
Both are equally correct; they're describing the same mechanism.

B is closer — schemas prevent shape errors, but required fields with absent source values still drive the model to fabricate. Nullable fields let Claude return `null` honestly. Both shape enforcement AND nullable-field design are needed for the full picture.
explanations: Schemas don't prevent semantic fabrication.
No such auto-detection.
They describe different mechanisms with different scopes.
Correct. Schema enforces shape; nullable fields prevent the fabrication-to-satisfy-required incentive.

question: A skeptical reviewer says: 'Forcing tool selection with `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"X"}` is the same as `tool_choice: "any"` when only tool X is registered, so always use "any" for simplicity.' What's the most defensible counter?
options: They produce different latency profiles.

Forced selection is explicit about which schema is intended, future-proof against later tool additions (a new tool wouldn't accidentally be picked), and clearer to readers reviewing the code; `"any"` is a strictly weaker statement.
`"any"` doesn't actually force a tool call; only forced does.
The Anthropic API rejects `"any"` when only one tool is registered.
explanations: Latency is the same.
Correct. Explicitness, future-proofing, and readability favour forced selection.
Both force a tool call; the difference is which.
`"any"` works fine with a single registered tool.

question: A pipeline force-calls `extract_metadata` on every turn. The team adds a follow-up enrichment step that needs Claude to either call an enrichment tool or summarise. What anti-pattern surfaces if `tool_choice` stays forced on the metadata tool throughout the conversation?
options: Metadata extraction silently fails on follow-up turns.
The harness drops the metadata payload because it's stale.

Claude re-extracts metadata every turn because forced selection re-fires the same tool, blocking enrichment and burning tokens; the fix is to relax `tool_choice` after the initial extraction (e.g., to `"auto"` so Claude can pick enrichment or summarise as appropriate).
The API rejects forced tool selection on multi-turn conversations.
explanations: Forced tool selection succeeds — it just fires repeatedly.
The harness keeps the payload; staleness isn't an API behaviour.
Correct. `tool_choice` is a per-turn parameter; leaving it forced re-fires the tool unnecessarily.
No such API restriction.
